title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

title: DrSai: an agentic AI system toward autonomous physics analysis workflows at BESIII
abstract: High Energy Physics (HEP) experiments like BESIII produce petabyte-scale data. Extracting physics results requires complex workflows (simulation, reconstruction, statistical analysis, etc.) that traditionally take experts months or years. Current manual methods are labor-intensive, prone to bias, and limit large-scale systematic scans. As data grows, this paradigm slows discovery. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a solution. Their natural language understanding and code generation capabilities allow them to interpret scientific tasks and integrate with HEP tools (e.g., ROOT, BOSS) to act as an "AI partner" for autonomous analysis. We present DrSai, an LLM-powered multi-agent system that translates natural language into rigorous physics workflows. As validation, DrSai performed large-scale re-measurements of ten J/psi decay branching fractions - without manual coding. It successfully navigated the real BESIII computing environment and produced results matching established benchmarks. The article details DrSai's architecture, the validation results, and performance evaluation. This work provides a blueprint for autonomous discovery, with relevance to other data-intensive fields like astronomy and genomics.

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a fine-tuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85.4%, comparable to ViT 82.6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86.3%; LLaVA 84.8%; ViT 84.7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86.3% and 85.9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.

title: Not All Gap Correction Helps: A Geometric View of External Information in LLM Inference
abstract: Providing external information beyond the query is a common way to improve large language model (LLM) inference, as seen in in-context learning (ICL), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and memory-based methods (Mem). Existing work increasingly suggests that useful external information should compensate for the gap between LLMs and user queries, implicitly assuming that stronger gap-correction can lead to better performance. In this paper, we challenge this assumption and show that more gap-corrective external information can instead harm performance. We analyze this phenomenon in Transformers through the lens of reasoning error, defined as the difference between the predicted answer vector and the ground-truth answer vector. Our analysis reveals that external information can be not only under-corrective but also over-corrective, where excessively strong correction increases reasoning error. We further show that the induced correction vector is jointly determined by attention and the complementarity between the external information and the query, and derive conditions under which information is properly corrective in both direction and magnitude. Experiments on four mainstream LLMs and seven reasoning benchmarks across ICL, RAG, and Mem validate our theory and support a theory-guided information selection method.

title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
abstract: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes
abstract: Objective Negative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institution's data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. Methods Four LLM agents operate on an institution's Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospital's electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. Results MENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was {kappa}=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. Conclusion Combining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone. Restricting reasoning to discordant candidates kept computation time below 40% of that with reasoning in all agents. Every decision comes with its evidence and rationale for investigators' final review.

title: Mobility-Aware Task Offloading in Mobile Edge Computing-Empowered Space-Air-Ground Integrated Internet-of-Things Networks
abstract: Mobile edge computing (MEC)-empowered spaceair-ground integrated Internet-of-Things (IoT) networks (SAGIINs) provide a promising solution for computation-intensive tasks generated by mobile IoT devices (IDs). However, task offloading in SAGIINs is challenging due to time-varying IDto-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) channels, intermittent LEO satellite service availability, and the coupling among UAV trajectory, communication, computation, and energy decisions. This paper investigates an energy-efficient task offloading and UAV trajectory planning problem in an MEC-empowered SAGIIN, where one UAV acts as both an aerial relay and an MEC server, and multiple LEO satellites provide supplementary computing resources. The UAV trajectory planning, task splitting, and computing resource allocation are jointly optimized to minimize the total system energy consumption under task completion, communication, computation, flight region, and satellite service window constraints. The resulting non-convex problem is decomposed into a UAV trajectory planning subproblem and a task splitting and computing resource allocation subproblem. To solve the former, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-assisted large language model (LLM)-enhanced deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm, termed RLD, is proposed. The latter is shown to be convex and can be solved by using CVXPY for a given UAV trajectory. A weighted retrieval score is further designed to balance ID mobility-pattern similarity and historical UAV trajectory energy performance. Simulation results show that RLD completes all computational tasks in previously unseen test scenarios while consuming less total energy than the benchmark algorithms.

title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.

title: Beyond Sequence and Structure: Pretraining PLMs on Continuous Biophysical Fields
abstract: We introduce the Biophysical Transformer, a protein language model that adds continuous biophysical fields as a third pretraining signal beside sequence and structure. A Poisson-Boltzmann solver computes the electrostatic potential around each three-residue token, and the model learns to predict it from sequence alone. A rotationally invariant spherical-harmonic descriptor serves as the loss target, eliminating the need for frame alignment during training and for coordinates at inference. Against a matched, one-flag control on the FLIP Meltome thermostability benchmark, the field objective raises Spearman correlation on every trained head of both human splits.The gain on human survives residualizing dipeptide composition under two architecturally different readouts and survives removing the test proteins that overlap the pretraining corpus. No effect survives on the organism-mixed split. At 1.1M parameters, both the Biophysical Transformer and its sequence-only control exceed FLIP's one-hot CNN and untrained-ESM baselines on every split. All results rest on a single pretraining run per arm,and the current design does not separate field content from generic regularization.

title: AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation
abstract: Scientific research proceeds through iterative cycles of hypothesis generation, experiment design, execution, and revision. AI agents can automate parts of this process, but existing approaches typically follow a single research trajectory or coordinate through a central planner with fixed objectives. As a result, they struggle to sustain parallel exploration, adapt as experimental evidence changes, or preserve knowledge of failed directions over long-running experiments. We introduce AutoScientists, a decentralized team of AI agents for long-running computational scientific experimentation. Agents interpret a shared experimental state, self-organize into teams around promising hypotheses, critique proposals before using experimental compute, and share successes and failures to reduce redundant exploration. Under matched experimental budgets, AutoScientists improves over prior AI agents across biomedical machine learning, language-model training optimization, and protein fitness prediction. On BioML-Bench, spanning biomedical imaging, protein engineering, single-cell omics, and drug discovery, AutoScientists achieves a mean leaderboard percentile of 74.4% across 24 tasks, improving over the strongest AI agent by +8.33%. On GPT training optimization, AutoScientists reaches a target validation bits-per-byte 1.9x faster than Autoresearch and continues discovering improvements from a starting champion where the single-agent approach finds none (7 vs. 0 accepted improvements). On ProteinGym fitness prediction, AutoScientists discovers a method for ACE2-Spike binding that improves over the current state-of-the-art model by +12.5% in Spearman correlation. Applied without modification across all 217 ProteinGym assays, the same method improves over the prior state of the art by +6.5% (Spearman correlation).

title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

title: VArify: A Visual Analytics System for Verifying Knowledge Enhanced Large Language Model Responses in Food Science
abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) grounds Large Language Model (LLM) responses in structured, domain-specific knowledge. However, verification remains difficult because errors can arise at multiple layers: an answer may not be faithful to its retrieved context, the retrieval pipeline may select irrelevant evidence, and the knowledge graph may omit relevant facts or contain incorrect triplets. We present VArify, a visual analytics system for food-science researchers to inspect and repair these layers in a GraphRAG workflow. A formative study with five participants using a conventional chat-and-table interface revealed behaviors reflecting answer anchoring, over-trust, and difficulty tracing multi-hop relationships. In response, VArify combines an evidence-first answer reveal with coordinated chat and hierarchical graph views, provenance inspection, and subquery editing. It connects the generated answer, the retrieval state, and the provenance-linked graph so that researchers can trace discrepancies across them and repair the retrieved context. From a qualitative system-use study on six food science researchers, we characterize how they scrutinize GraphRAG evidence with progressive visual inspection. Our study also reveals an important verification boundary: information absent from both retrieval and a user's knowledge remains unverifiable. We discuss the broader role of visualization in supporting oversight of LLM responses and outline future research directions.

title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents. The project repository is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
abstract: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.

title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2. Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

title: An auditable harness for biomolecular dynamics simulations by AI agents
abstract: AI agents now generate biological hypotheses faster than they can be tested. Hypotheses stated at the atomic level can be examined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For new questions without a reference, trust in an agent-run simulation rests on a tool-written process record, not the agent's account. Existing MD agents leave this record to the language model. Here we present MDClaw, a harness whose validating tools and directed acyclic graph (DAG) check stages before execution and record every simulation stage. On MDDataBench, which grades outputs against deposited simulations, four open-weight models with MDClaw passed all three runs on 81-100% of 31 test systems. The DAG complements this outcome check. An ablation without the DAG revealed 11 successful runs that had skipped minimization or equilibration, or simulated a different structure. MDClaw carried questions from human and AI scientists through simulation to trajectories traceable to their inputs and settings.

title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

title: Adaptive Retrieval, Selective Answers: Evaluating Conformal Factuality in Agentic RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the grounding of language-model responses through external evidence, yet retrieved information alone does not ensure factual support for generated claims. In agentic RAG, evidence acquisition is further complicated by adaptive retrieval decisions, where an agent iteratively determines whether to retrieve additional information or terminate the search. We investigate how conformal factuality can be applied in this setting to improve the reliability of generated responses. We formalize the agent-driven retrieval process and characterize a query-aware relevance-scoring formulation that accounts for evidence collected across successive retrieval decisions. Building on this formulation, we evaluate post-generation conformal claim filtering using GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B across HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Our experiments demonstrate that increasingly stringent conformal targets are consistently associated with higher observed response-level factual support, accompanied by reductions in claim retention and non-empty response coverage. The extent of these trade-offs varies across models and datasets, highlighting the importance of jointly evaluating factual reliability and answer availability. These findings establish an empirical foundation for studying conformal factuality in agent-driven retrieval systems and motivate further investigation into improving the reliability of their generated responses.

title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

title: ThermoMutDB 2.0: semiautomated literature curation and structural enrichment of thermostability data for protein mutations.
abstract: Experimental measurements of protein thermodynamic stability are essential for understanding the relationship between protein structure and function, the molecular consequences of mutations, and their potential implications for protein malfunction and disease. However, extracting these data from the literature remains constrained by labor-intensive manual curation. Here, we present ThermoMutDB 2.0, a scalable framework for semiautomated literature curation and systematic structural enrichment. It introduces a major architectural redesign that integrates a large language model with rule-based entity recognition to identify and prioritize publications reporting experimentally measured effects of protein mutations on thermostability, while retaining expert validation as the final curation step. Complementing this literature-processing workflow, ThermoMutDB 2.0 systematically enriches curated mutations with mutant structural models, enabling interactive three-dimensional contextualization of experimentally derived thermodynamic data. Applied to the literature retrieved from January 1976 to the most recent search update in 2026, the pipeline screened 5,934 candidate publications and prioritized 254 for expert review, resulting in the incorporation of 102 articles and 1763 new entries. Rather than representing a simple expansion of database content, ThermoMutDB 2.0 establishes an extensible human-in-the-loop architecture in which automated literature triage, expert curation, and structural modeling operate as an integrated workflow. This redesign provides a sustainable foundation for continuous database maintenance and for linking experimental protein stability measurements with their structural context (available at http://thermomutdb.pathotrack.health/).

title: CPDD: Adapting an autoregressive DNA language model for bidirectional phage genome modeling
abstract: Autoregressive DNA language models generate sequences ef[fi]ciently from left to right, but many genome-analysis and sequence-editing problems are naturally conditioned on both [fl]anks. We introduce CreatiPhage, a 144.5M-parameter autoregressive DNA language model for bacteriophages, and its diffusion extension, CreatiPhage Diffusion DNA-LM (CPDD). CPDD is a 147.5M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model initialized from the six-epoch CreatiPhage checkpoint. CPDD retains the pretrained Transformer, block attention residuals, and Engram conditional memory, while introducing non-causal attention, a MASK-aware base-5 Engram, centered depthwise convolution, and position-aligned nucleotide readout. Training combines masked and GIDD-style uniformly substituted bases with nucleotide- and amino-acid-level losses over a 10 kb, 32 kb, and whole-source context curriculum. On a screened panel of 522 phage CDSs, CPDD achieves higher random-mask restoration accuracy than a comparable diffusion model and performs well above codon-level references. In a mixed-corruption test, it restores 42.4% of visible incorrect bases. Frozen CPDD representations also support infA [fi]tness prediction and seven-class phage virion protein subtype classi[fi]cation. Controlled evaluations further characterize how restoration depends on visible context and identify opportunities to improve longer-range sequence recovery. Together, these results support scaffold-conditioned sequence modeling as a step towards modular design of phage genomes.

title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. As a first step in developing and demonstrating the methodology, we compared study-specific implementations of SmED 5.4.11 accessed via API and Infermedica Engine API via Microsoft Azure Healthcare Agent Service with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. The manufacturers of SmED and Infermedica offer MDR-certified Class IIb triage products, but these certified products were not directly evaluated. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories-emergency, acute, and not urgent-and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

title: EZpred: Improving Deep Learning-Based Enzyme Function Prediction Using Unlabeled Sequence Homologs.
abstract: Features extracted from sequence homologs significantly enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based protein structure prediction. Indeed, homolog-aware models such as AlphaFold generally produce more accurate protein structures compared to single sequence-based methods like ESMfold. In contrast, features from sequence homologs are seldom employed for deep learning-based prediction of the biological functions of a protein, such as Gene Ontology terms or Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers. Although a small number of models also incorporate function labels from sequence homologs, they cannot utilize features extracted from homologs that lack function labels. To address this gap, we developed EZpred, which is the first deep learning model to use sequence homologs by extracting their sequence features while ignoring any function labels. Starting with the target sequence and homologs identified by MMseqs2, EZpred extracts sequence features using the ESM-C protein language model. These features are then fed into a deep learning model to predict the EC numbers of the target protein. For test enzymes with < 30% sequence identity to any training proteins, the F1-score of EZpred EC number prediction is at least 34% higher than state-of-the-art EC number prediction models. These results demonstrate the strong positive impact of sequence homologs in deep learning-based enzyme function prediction.

title: LLM Embeddings Complement Theory-Driven Language Features and Cognitive Scores for APOE4 and Aβ Prediction
abstract: Spontaneous language offers a scalable, noninvasive approach for identifying biological indicators of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD). We examined prediction of APOE4 carrier status and cerebral amyloid-beta burden using Cookie Theft picture descriptions from two cohorts of Hebrew- and English-speaking participants (IRAP, N=134; WRAP, N=1,541). Amyloid-beta burden was classified using lowest-quartile, median, and highest-quartile cutoffs, capturing accumulation below conventional amyloid-positivity thresholds. We compared embeddings from pretrained large language models (LLMs) with standard cognitive test scores, reflecting conventional clinical assessment, and theory-driven linguistic features, reflecting traditional language analysis. Embedding-based models achieved the highest F1 scores among constituent models in five of eight tasks involving APOE4 status and global amyloid-beta burden. High prediction disagreement suggested complementary signals across approaches. An any-positive ensemble significantly outperformed every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline across all eight tasks, and significantly outperformed all constituent models in 21 of 24 regional amyloid-beta tasks. These findings highlight the complementarity of LLM-based, theory-driven, and cognitive measures for predicting AD-related genetic risk and amyloid pathology, and support further investigation of their potential for early screening approaches.

title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach
abstract: Background: Proper adoption of AI in emergency medicine necessitate thorough and rigorous appraisal. Classic benchmarks, which rely heavily on basic question-and-answer formats, though dominating the benchmarking field of LLM usage in medicine, have proven inadequate in assessing the full spectrum of skills incumbent upon an agent in healthcare. Methods: We propose an intricate benchmarking scheme in which the skill set required of an emergency physician is tested and quantified. Our benchmarking structure is 3-fold: skills such as history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and empathy are evaluated by an emergency medicine expert, while the same expertise is scored by an intern from the perspective of a patient, through what we call a simulated emergency room visit. A comprehensive written examination is also utilized to measure general emergency medicine knowledge. Results: Eight LLMs were benchmarked against each other and in contrast to nine emergency medical doctors. Our findings indicate that the AI models significantly outperformed human physicians across several key domains, including history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment planning. Furthermore, the models demonstrated superior performance in comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy. When comparing AI models against each other, performance advantages were marginal during simulated emergency room visits and were mostly pronounced during the written examination. Conclusion: AI models demonstrate a clear advantage over human physicians across a diverse range of emergency medicine competencies. The proposed benchmarking scheme provides a comprehensive metric for a thorough evaluation of medical skill set, furthering validation, adaptation, and utilization of AI in emergency medicine.

title: ragR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and RAG Assessment in R
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines document retrieval with large language models (LLMs) to produce responses grounded in external evidence. While several R packages support core components of RAG workflows, integrated evaluation of RAG systems in R remains limited and is often conducted through Python-based tools, most notably the RAG assessment (RAGAS) framework. To address this gap, we introduce ragR, an R package that unifies document ingestion, embedding and vector storage, similarity-based retrieval, grounded generation, structured question-answer logging, and RAGAS-style evaluation within a single R-native workflow. Its evaluation module, ragR-RAGAS, uses an LLM as a judge to score four core RAGAS metrics: context precision, context recall, faithfulness, and answer relevance. To assess the credibility of these automated judgments, we compared ragR-RAGAS with two independent human annotators on three document collections. The human annotators demonstrated consistently high agreement, and ragR-RAGAS generally aligned with their judgments, although discrepancies were more pronounced for context precision and the identification of unsupported statements. By integrating RAG construction and evaluation within a reproducible workflow in R, ragR provides a practical framework for research, teaching, and moderate-scale experimentation on RAG systems entirely within the R ecosystem.

title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
abstract: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Aware Framework for Trustworthy Molecular Property Prediction
abstract: Molecular property prediction is fundamental to computational chemistry and drug formulation research, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across datasets, properties, and evaluation protocols, limiting systematic evaluation of model generalization. We introduce Chem World, a large-scale benchmark integrating 17 public datasets with over 800,000 molecular and chemical-system instances across 10 property tracks, covering single-molecule and multi-component systems, including drug solubility. Chem World provides a unified testbed for evaluating molecular representations and compositional modeling across diverse chemical properties. Building on the benchmark, we propose PACM (Physics-Aware Compositional Modeling), which combines molecular representations with composition-aware modeling and domain-specific physical constraints. Extensive experiments show that molecular language models provide strong and transferable representations, while PACM consistently improves prediction across diverse chemical systems. Chem World and our PACM-powered drug-property prediction Agent support generalizable chemical modeling and offer a foundation for AI-assisted biomedical research and drug formulation development.

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

title: Deep Learning-Enabled Magnetic Bead-Capture Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization Enables Multiplex Identification and Digital Counting of Pathogenic Bacteria.
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most prevalent infectious diseases worldwide. For complicated and antimicrobial-resistant cases, timely diagnosis is critical for guiding targeted therapy and improving patient outcomes. While conventional urine culture suffers from prolonged turnaround times and low positive detection rates, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) has emerged as a rapid, highly specific alternative. However, its clinical application remains hindered by complicated sample pretreatment, insufficient sensitivity that often requires pre-enrichment by culture, and subjective bias in manual interpretation. To address these bottlenecks, we developed deep learning-enabled magnetic bead-capture fluorescence in situ hybridization (DeepMag-FISH), a culture-free platform that employs artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted digital counting for rapid identification and single-bacterium enumeration of pathogens. We adopted soluble β2-glycoprotein I (sβ2GPI)-coated magnetic beads for efficient pathogen enrichment, and utilized a modular dual-probe labeling strategy for multiplexed hybridization, thus enabling highly specific molecular labeling. Additionally, we integrated this sample processing pipeline with a YOLOv11-based deep learning framework for automatic multiscale feature extraction and precise single-bacterium counting. Validated using spiked urine specimens, DeepMag-FISH clearly differentiated Escherichia coli, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Klebsiella pneumoniae with negligible spectral crosstalk. The platform reaches a detection capability of 30 CFU/mL, completing the entire workflow, including all magnetic separation and washing steps, within approximately 3.5 h. By combining magnetic bead-based pathogen enrichment with AI-driven image analysis, this approach mitigates matrix interference and subjective bias in conventional methods, offering a rapid and quantitative approach for pathogen detection in spiked urine samples. Beyond UTI management, DeepMag-FISH may also be explored for potential applications in other fields, such as bloodstream infection diagnosis and food safety monitoring.

title: PDO Drug Screening Data for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
abstract: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is critically important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Currently, most DRP models are developed using drug screening data from immortalized cancer cell lines, which can differ substantially from patient tumors at the genomic and molecular levels, even though patient tumor response is the ultimate prediction target. To help bridge this gap and bring DRP models closer to their intended clinical application, we conducted four drug screening studies using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which more faithfully recapitulate patient tumors than immortalized cell lines. These studies generated data for improving and evaluating DRP models, including multi-omics profiles of PDO lines, drug feature data, and treatment response measurements. Using these data, we retrained and evaluated multiple publicly available DRP models under three model-building scenarios: training models using cell line data only, training models using combined cell line and PDO data, and pretraining models on cell line data followed by fine-tuning on PDO data. We then evaluated and compared model prediction performance on PDOs across these analysis scenarios. In addition, we also assessed the consistency of drug screening viability data generated by different laboratories using different assay technologies and/or experimental protocols.

title: CRINN: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms have become increasingly critical for recent AI applications, particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agent-based LLM applications. In this paper, we present CRINN, a new paradigm for ANNS algorithms. CRINN treats ANNS optimization as a reinforcement learning problem where execution speed serves as the reward signal. This approach enables the automatic generation of progressively faster ANNS implementations while maintaining accuracy constraints. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates CRINN's effectiveness across six widely-used NNS benchmark datasets. When compared against state-of-the-art open-source ANNS algorithms, CRINN achieves best performance on three of them (GIST-960-Euclidean, MNIST-784-Euclidean, and GloVe-25-angular), and tied for first place on two of them (SIFT-128-Euclidean and GloVe-25-angular). The implications of CRINN's success reach well beyond ANNS optimization: It validates that LLMs augmented with reinforcement learning can function as an effective tool for automating sophisticated algorithmic optimizations that demand specialized knowledge and labor-intensive manual refinement. Code can be found at https://github.com/ornith-ai/CRINN

title: Privilege and confidentiality in generative AI workflows
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) systems store and process client data in three distinct ways: in the model's parameters through training and memorisation, in the context window during a live session, and in knowledge databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Each mode creates different and often counter-intuitive risks to confidentiality and legal professional privilege, and each calls for specific governance responses. Drawing on the first English and American decisions to address privilege and generative AI, UK and Munir v Secretary of State for the Home Department and United States v Heppner, on the orthodox privilege authorities against which those decisions must be read, and on recent computer science research, we explain the three modes of data storage and processing in terms accessible to practitioners and analyse the legal consequences of each. We then situate the analysis within the regulatory framework governing solicitors in England and Wales and within the ordinary principles of professional negligence, arguing that the standard of effective information governance (and with it the benchmark against which negligence and misconduct will be measured) is changing. Although we write primarily for SRA-regulated practitioners, our data-governance analysis is framed to extend to any jurisdiction in which the protection of privilege or professional secrecy depends on demonstrable confidentiality. The ultimate aim of this article is to help legal services professionals understand salient data leakage risks in GenAI systems and thereby facilitate a more responsible deployment of GenAI on client data and other sensitive material.

title: Food Critic: An Agentic Visualization System for Auditable Restaurant-Safety Reasoning
abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly being embedded into visualization systems that can search data, invoke tools, summarize evidence, and produce recommendations. However, when agents rely solely on their own knowledge, the visualization problem is not only whether the agent provides a useful answer, but also whether users can inspect how that answer is grounded. We present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system for diners' restaurant decision support that integrates public health inspection records with crowd review data. The system grounds agents under three conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval- augmented agent with access to food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. Food Critic externalizes the agent's reasoning within these groundings as inspectable visual evidence. We evaluate LLM models with several use cases under each grounding of our agentic system. Our work positions restaurant choice as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning, and the design of visual interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.

title: NEVEN: An Open-Source Polyglot Infrastructure Bridging Statistical Computing and Spreadsheet Workflows for Reproducible Research
abstract: We present NEVEN, an open-source infrastructure that embeds R, Julia, Python, Quarto, and JavaScript visualization libraries into Excel through native worksheet formulas. Users run econometric estimators, solve differential equations, and compile reproducible reports using expressions such as =R.MR_Lineal(...), =J.Optimize(...), and =P.ai_call(...), without procedural programming or external application switching. The platform offers over 70 R statistical procedures, 70 high-level Julia procedures backed by more than 200 mathematical functions, and full Python 3 integration for statistical computing and numerical analysis. Each language runtime runs in an independent operating-system process connected to the Excel XLL host via Windows Named Pipes and Protocol Buffers. Fatal errors terminate only the affected child process, leaving Excel operational. A static security sandbox checks user code against 25-30 restricted patterns per language, blocking shell execution, file deletion, unauthorized network access, and dynamic evaluation through five bypass-prevention mechanisms validated by 133 tests. An embedded WebView2 engine displays interactive Plotly charts, D3.js network and hierarchical visualizations, Leaflet maps, pivot tables, LaTeX notation, PDF documents, and Pluto.jl reactive notebooks through a unified formula, =NEVEN.v(). The docked NEVEN Studio environment offers nine specialized modules, including a Chart Gallery with 325 templates, an in-memory DuckDB SQL console, a retrieval-augmented AI assistant, and a multi-language script editor with English and Spanish localization. Econometric estimates match published benchmarks to four decimal places, while Julia linear algebra decompositions achieve machine-precision accuracy (relative error below 10^-14). Released under GNU General Public License v3, NEVEN includes 342 automated unit, property-based, and integration tests.

title: Precision Neurology in Alzheimer's Disease: Genomics to Drug Optimization for Effective Therapeutic Intervention.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits high clinical and biological heterogeneity, which complicates the development of one-size-fits-all therapeutic strategies. Standard trial designs can mask subgroup-specific effects, highlighting the need to move towards precision neurology entailing multisystem genomics, biomarkers, and artificial intelligence (AI) integrative signals. The aim of the study is to critically synthesize and evaluate emerging strategies for drug optimization and individual therapeutic algorithms informed by genomic architecture, pharmacogenomics (PGx), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) with the opinion to resolve the controversy and unanswered question. Amplify the convergence into amyloid processing, lipid metabolism, and innate immunity seen from monogenic mutations and over 80 GWAS risk loci. Genotyping of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 variants permits pharmacogenomic stratifications for the optimization of cholinesterase inhibitor and psychotropic dosing, thereby reducing adverse events. Variants of the alleles APOE ε4 and immune-related factors (e.g., FCGR3A) are significant in predicting the effects of ARIA associated with amyloid on anti-amyloid immunotherapy outcomes. PRS and deep phenotyping (including digital and fluid-based biomarkers) allow for the identification of unique biological endotypes (e.g., tau-dominant vs. vascular-inflammatory) that improve clinical trial enrichment and prognostication. This framework delineates molecular endotypes and translates CYP2D6 or APOE stratification into drug dosing and ARIA risk predictions. These biomarker-driven strategies shift AD management from a passive, reactive therapeutic scheme to an active, personalized one. Utilization of high-dimensional data streams via AI-driven learning health systems converts AD management from a reactive, symptom-based model to that which is proactive and hallmark biomarker-driven precision.

title: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma.
abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. If and how tumor plasticity of EWS::FLI1-regulated transcriptional signatures contributes to disease progression is not known. To address this, we utilized a single-cell co-assay of RNA and chromatin accessibility (ATAC) sequencing to identify gene regulatory networks in EwS. By comprehensively characterizing regulatory elements across cell lines, we identified multiple unique modules of gene regulation. Differential usage and prevalence of these modules was evident across cell lines, associated with distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures, and in specific cases, modifiable by exogenous TGF-β. When we examined primary EwS patient tumors, we observed these same regulatory modules were variably enriched both across and within tumors, highlighting the existence of intratumoral heterogeneity in gene regulatory networks. Our findings demonstrate that multiple, co-existing transcriptional programs shape the phenotypic diversity of EwS and suggest that the balance between these networks may have important implications for clinical outcomes and targeted therapy development.

title: CanViT: Toward Active-Vision Foundation Models
abstract: Active computer vision promises efficient, biologically plausible perception through sequential, localized glimpses, but lacks scalable general-purpose architectures and pretraining pipelines, leaving Active-Vision Foundation Models (AVFMs) underexplored. We introduce the Canvas Vision Transformer (CanViT), the first task- and policy-agnostic AVFM. CanViT uses scene-relative RoPE to bind a retinotopic Vision Transformer backbone and a spatiotopic scene-wide latent workspace, the canvas. Efficient interaction with this high-capacity working memory is supported by Canvas Attention, a novel asymmetric cross-attention mechanism. We decouple thinking (backbone-level) and memory (canvas-level), eliminating canvas-side self-attention and fully-connected layers to achieve fast sequential inference and scalability to high output resolutions. We propose a label-free active vision pretraining scheme, policy-agnostic passive-to-active dense latent distillation: reconstructing scene-wide DINOv3 embeddings from sequences of low-resolution glimpses with randomized locations, zoom levels, and lengths. We pretrain CanViT-B from a random initialization on 13.2 million ImageNet-21k scenes and 1 billion random glimpses, in 166 hours on a single H100. On ADE20K segmentation, a frozen CanViT-B achieves 38.5% mIoU in a single low-resolution glimpse, outperforming the best active model's 27.6% with 20x fewer inference FLOPs as well as its FLOP- or input-matched DINOv3 teacher. Given additional glimpses, CanViT-B reaches 45.9% ADE20K mIoU. On ImageNet-1k classification, CanViT-B also sets a new active-vision state of the art, with 84.5% top-1 accuracy after fine-tuning. CanViT generalizes to longer rollouts, larger scenes, and new policies. Our work narrows the wide gap between passive and active computer vision, demonstrating the potential of task- and policy-agnostic AVFM pretraining.
